parts: [{"label":"A","letter":"A","text":"Which line has passed through the middle of the territory of Bangladesh?","marks":1,"answer":"The Tropic of Cancer passes through (23°.5°) over the middle of Bangladesh.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"B","letter":"B","text":"Why do rivers of Bangladesh flow towards the Bay of Bengal?","marks":2,"answer":"Since the region of Bangladesh possesses a gradual slanting ground from the North towards the South, all the rivers in the country flow from the North to the South towards the Bay of Bengal.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Explain the formation of land configuration of the region marked with ‘A’ in the figure.","marks":3,"answer":"The region marked ‘A’ on the map is the flights of steps or plains from the Pleistocene age. The region consists of around 8% of land in Bangladesh. Pleistocene age is called the time before approximately 25,000 years. These flights of steps are assumed to have been formed by the glacial floods during that time. The flights of steps of the Pleistocene age may be divided into three categories. Those are - the Barendra Bhumi, the Modhupur and Bhavaler Gar and the Lalmai Hill. The Barendra Bhumi includes some regions in Naogaon, Rajshahi, Bogra, Joypurhat, Rangpur and Dinajpur districts. Area of Barendra Bhumi is 9320 square kilometers. Soil in these areas is of grey and red colours. The soil is less humid in these areas. Paddy and jute grow in the soil of these areas. However, the land in the Barendra Bhumi is ideal for the cultivation of mango and litchi. Mangoes from Barendra Bhumi are famous across Bangladesh. The Modhupur and Bhavaler Gar consist of some areas in Mymensingh, Tangail, Gazipur and Dhaka districts. The Lalmai hills extend from Lalmai, about 8 kilometers west of Cumilla, to Moynamoti.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"What will be observed more in the region marked with ‘B’ & ‘C’ in the figure? Give arguments in support of your answer.","marks":4,"answer":"The area marked ‘B’ on the map is Khagrachhari, a hill tract region, and the area marked ‘C’ is Narsingdi. It is a plain land. Since Narsingdi is the plain land among the two areas, more factories and higher population density would be located in Narsingdi. According to the stimulus, Narsingdi is a plain land while Khagrachhari is a hill tract and forest region. Therefore, from a geographical aspect, Narsingdi is more suitable for developing human settlements. On the other hand, the regions in Bangladesh where mineral resources are found have been inhabited by workers who went there to work and develop settlements. Narsingdi is more populated compared to Khagrachhari due to this reason. These human settlements are developed centering mineral, agricultural, forestry and livestock resources in the areas. Many associated industries have gradually developed beside the main industries in these areas. As the industries and trade flourished over time, the areas turned more populous depending on the main industries. Therefore, Narsingdi being a plain land is one such densely populated district. Besides Narsingdi, human settlements also developed as industrialization flourished in other areas including Teigaon, Tongi, Khulna, Chattogram, etc. Communication between different areas becomes easier if roads, railways and inland waterways are developed. As a result, the areas become populated.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

Due to geographical location, Bangladesh is located near the boundary of the Indian and European plates. Due to this, the probability of earthquake in Bangladesh is high. Due to the topography and internal structure, seismic forces are active in Bangladesh and result in earthquakes. Again, due to man-made and natural reasons, some parts of the country are going down, some parts are swelling. Thus the possibility of earthquakes increases as a result of swelling. Explain it.","marks":3,"answer":"The region traveled by Lipi indicates the plains of the Pleistocene age of Bangladesh. The flights of the plains of Pleistocene age comprise about 8% of the total volume of land of Bangladesh. Approximately, the Pleistocene age is the age before 25000 years. It is guessed that such flights of steps were formed due to originating of floods with the internally melted icy waters of that period. The flights steps of the Pleistocene age may be divided into three categories – The Barendra Bhumi, The Modhupur and Bhavaler Gar and the Lalmai Hill. The Barendra Bhumi comprises of some parts of the districts of Naogaon, Rajshahi, Bogra, Joypurhat, Rangpur and a particular region of the district of Dinajpur. This region has an area of 9320 Square kilometers. The soils of these areas are of grey, and red colors. The countryards of the Modhupur and Bhaval comprise of some parts of the districts of Mymensingh, Tangail and Gazipur. It possesses a volume near about 4103 square kilometres and soils here possess radish and grey hues. The Lalmai Hill stretched from Lalmai of Cumilla to Moynamati. It possesses an area of 34 square kilometres. In the scenario-1 of the stem, Lipi goes to Somapura Mahavihara on a study tour and is fascinated by noticing the red-colored soil there. Lipi's travelled, Somapura Mahavihara is located in Naogaon district and belongs to Barendra Bhumi. And Barendra Bhumi is a plain formed during the Pleistocene. So it can be said that the region traveled by Lipi indicates the plains of the Pleistocene age.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"Is there any difference in the sector of agricultural production between the visited area of Mr. Khademul and the study tour area of Lipi? Give opinion.","marks":4,"answer":"Yes, there is a difference in agricultural production between the Tertiary hilly areas seen by Khademul in the stem and the plains of the Pleistocene age of Bangladesh of Lipi's study tour. About 12% of the total land area of Bangladesh is made up of Tertiary hilly areas. The hills of this area can be divided into two categories. Such as- The hills of the south-eastern region and the hills of the north-eastern region. The forests in these hilly regions are known as tropical evergreen and deciduous forest areas. The leaves of these forest trees do not bloom or fall at the same time. That is why these forests are green throughout the year. The hills of the Tertiary age are composed of sandstone, clay and shell-stone. The features of the area seen by Khademul indicate the hills of Tertiary age. On the other hand, the Somapura Mahavihara visited by Lipi is located in Naogaon. This area is included in the flights of steps/the plains of the Pleistocene age. The hills of the Tertiary age seen by Khademul of the stem are mainly hilly areas. The soil here is not fertile as it consists of sandstone, clay and shell-stone. As the land is up and down, it is almost impossible to produce crops in these areas. In these regions, Jhum cultivation produces a small amount of agriculture. On the other hand, the Pleistocene plains seen by Lipi are very suitable for agriculture. The soil of this region is very fertile. As a result, various crops including rice, wheat, maize, jute, mustard, sugarcane and vegetables are grown in these areas throughout the year. However, water shortage occurs in this region during winter and summer. As a result, agricultural production is somewhat disrupted at the time. It can be seen from the above discussion that the hilly area in the Tertiary age seen by Khademul is not very suitable for agricultural production. And the Pleistocene plains traveled by Lipi produced a variety of crops as it is suitable for agricultural production.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

The flights of the plains of Pleistocene Terrace comprise about 8% of the total volume of land of Bangladesh. Approximately, the Pleistocene age is the age before 25000 years. The courtyards of the Modhupur and Bhaval comprise of some parts of the districts of Mymensingh, Tangail and Gazipur and some parts of Dhaka. Bangladesh possesses a vast land comprising about 80% of the total volume washed by river water. A number of rivers flow over the plains. Due to the influence of river flows and floods, alluvium has accumulated in the basin and the land has become very fertile. This plain is known as recent flood plain. The area of this floodplain is 1,24,266 square kilometers. The soil layer of the entire plain is very deep and the land is very fertile. Recent flood plains can be divided into several parts. This floodplain consists of parts of different districts like Dhaka, Tangail, Cumilla, Noakhali, Chandpur, Laxmipur, Feni, etc. Coastal delta plains and water course level land belong to this category. Greater Khulna, Barisal and the southern part of Dhaka Division are made up of riverine alluvium and the region is quite fertile. The areas marked 'C' on the map of the stem are Faridpur and Gopalganj. Agriculture is easy due to numerous small and big rivers in this region. During floods, these rivers carry silt and increase soil fertility. Cultivation is easy here and the yield is high. So it can be said that the area marked 'C' of the stem plays an important role in crop production, fisheries and navigation.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

parts: [{"label":"A","letter":"A","text":"What is called climate?","marks":1,"answer":"The daily average state of climate's constituent pervading in a vast region is called climate.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"B","letter":"B","text":"Why is agricultural land decreasing?","marks":2,"answer":"The amount of agricultural land in Bangladesh is decreasing due to population growth. Bangladesh is an overpopulated country. The population is much larger than the size of the country. Due to the increase in population, settlement is also increasing. But the amount of cultivable land in this country is much less than the requirement. As the population in our country continues to grow at an increasing rate, agricultural land is under constant pressure. As a result, new houses are being built on arable land. And this is why the amount of agricultural land is decreasing.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"In which season did Sumon go to visit Ripon's house? Explain.","marks":3,"answer":"Suman visited Ripon's house in the winter. The winter in Bangladesh lasts from November to February every year. At this time, as the sun is in the southern hemisphere, its rays fall obliquely on Bangladesh, and the amount of heat is reduced considerably. During this time, the temperature gradually decreases from the seacoast in the south to the north. January is the coldest month in Bangladesh. The average temperature in this month is about 20 degrees in Chittagong, 19.4 degrees in Noakhali, 18.3 degrees in Dhaka, 17.7 degrees in Bogra, and 16.6 degrees in Dinajpur. However, sometimes the temperature is lower in the northern region. In Scenario-1, Suman, a boy from Cox's Bazar, goes to his friend Ripon's house in the north of Bangladesh. At that time, the sun's rays fell diagonally across our country. At this time, the temperature in the northern region near Suman is much lower than in the southern region. Since the sun shines obliquely in the country in winter and the temperature in the north is much lower than in the south, it can therefore be said that Suman visited his friend Ripon's house in the winter.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"\"The season mentioned in Niloy's event is a blessing of agriculture of Bangladesh.\" Do you agree? Give logic in favour of your answer.","marks":4,"answer":"In Niloy's scenario, he mentions the summer season as a blessing for agriculture in Bangladesh, a comment I do not agree with. As can be seen in Scenario-2, Nilay feels quite hot while walking along the Padma River with his friend. But after a while, a cold wind started blowing from the west, and gradually it turned into a storm. This point in scenario-2 refers to the summer season. Not the summer season, but the monsoon season is a blessing for agriculture in Bangladesh. The temperature does not rise as much as it should because it rains a lot during the monsoon season. Due to heavy rainfall, the soil is very fertile during this time. It grows a variety of crops and fruits in abundance. Farmers in our country wait for monsoons for long days. Rain makes the soil more productive. So at this time, farmers plant various kinds of crops. Floods occur in the country as a result of heavy rainfall during the monsoon season. Flood waters carry alluvium in this country. This alluvium increases the fertility of agricultural land. It also improves crop production. Based on the above discussion, it can be said that not summer but the monsoon is a blessing for agriculture in Bangladesh.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

As the population of a country increases, so does the settlement. It reduces the amount of cultivable land. Agricultural lands were divided among heirs and fragmented. Identify and describe.","marks":3,"answer":"The traveled region of Lamia represents one of the geo-natural regions of Bangladesh, the Tertiary Age Hills. The mountain ranges formed during the Tertiary period about 2 million years ago due to the uplift of the Himalayas are called the Tertiary Mountains. This geo-natural region comprises about 12% of the total land area of Bangladesh. The hills of this region are divided into two parts. Namely, 1. South-Eastern Mountains and 2. North-Eastern Hills. In the eastern part of Rangamati, Khagrachari, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, and Chittagong districts, the Tertiary South Eastern Range is located. The highest peak in Bangladesh is located in the Tajiodong (Bijoy) region in the Bandarban district. Its height is 1231 meters. It was this mountain that Lamia visited. The stem's scenario 1 states that after the SSC exam, Lamia goes on a trip to the Nilgiris and Sajek and visits the highest mountain in Bangladesh. Compared to the above discussion, it can be understood that the places visited by her belong to the geological regions formed during the Tertiary period.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"\"The changes observed in scenario-2 are affecting the lives of people in Bangladesh,\"—Do you agree? Give arguments in favour of your opinion.","marks":4,"answer":"Climate change can be observed in scenario-2. I think that climate change is having various effects on the livelihood of the people of Bangladesh. Climate is the long-term average of the daily conditions of the weather elements over a large area. And the variation in climate that occurs with the seasons is called climate change. In stem's scenario-2, it can be seen that Abir's country has been experiencing heavy rains at the end of July without much rainfall in June for the past few years. Floods occur due to excessive rainfall in a short period of time. This variation in rainfall is indicative of climate change. Due to climate change, there have been many changes in the lives of the people of Bangladesh. For example, due to river erosion caused by climate change, about 4 lakh people have become homeless and have taken shelter in the city for their livelihood. As agricultural production is disrupted, ordinary farmers and laborers are migrating to cities in search of work. It causes family breakdowns. The safety of children, the elderly, and women is being disturbed. Due to climate change and failure to adapt to the environment, many animal species have become extinct, biodiversity has disappeared, and food production has decreased. This has increased hunger and poverty. The occupation of coastal fishermen is changing. Many fishermen seek employment in the city to earn a living. The livelihood of coastal people is somehow dependent on natural resources. The lives of the poor, very poor, middle-class, and rich people in these regions revolve around natural resources such as ponds, canals, land, gardens, trees, fish, etc. As a result of climate change, their livelihoods are being lost due to various disasters. Waterlogging, salinity, floods, inundation, storms, floods, storms, cyclones, etc. have affected people's livelihoods in many ways. Based on the above discussion, it can be said that climate change is affecting the livelihood of people in Bangladesh in various ways. Due to this, people's suffering is increasing day by day.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

parts: [{"label":"A","letter":"A","text":"What is called 'Kal Boishakhi'?","marks":1,"answer":"Storm that occurs during summer due to dry and cold air flowing from West and North-West direction is called Kal Boishakhi.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"B","letter":"B","text":"How can we save our rivers from the navigabilities problem?","marks":2,"answer":"River navigability problems can be eliminated by regularly dredging the river, not building unnecessary dams, pools, or culverts on the river, and maintaining the flow of water. Due to the construction of bridges and dams in the river, the accumulation of salt, and excess water extraction from the river, the navigability of the river has become a problem. Therefore, the river should be dug regularly to eliminate the navigability crisis. The construction of unnecessary dams, pools, and culverts should be discouraged. Besides, to maintain the flow of water, we have to take the initiative to build reservoirs.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"C","letter":"C","text":"Which season has been reflected in the stem? Explain.","marks":3,"answer":"The season that has been reflected in the stem bears the summer characteristics of the climate of Bangladesh. The summer in Bangladesh is from March to May. It is the hottest season in the country. Usually, the maximum temperature in this season is 38 degrees Celsius. And the minimum is 21 degrees Celsius. At this time, the temperature is gradually rising from the south to the north of the country due to the influence of the sea breeze. During summer, as the sun approaches the Tropic of Cancer in the Northern Hemisphere, the air pressure changes and the southwest monsoon blows over Bangladesh. At the same time, dry and cold air blows from the west and northwest. It creates a storm. This storm is called Kalbaisakhi which has been referred to by the stem. In the above-mentioned stem, Maya is seen sitting on the bank of the pond in front of the house in the afternoon of April. Young boys and girls were jumping into the pond to determine the temperature. She looked up and saw that the tree did not bear many mangoes this year. Hence, it can be said that the phenomenon of the season mentioned in the stem is similar to the summer season in Bangladesh.","image":null,"image_url":null},{"label":"D","letter":"D","text":"The events stated in the above stem are related simultaneously with our lives and living.—Analyze the statement.","marks":4,"answer":"“The events stated in the above stem are related simultaneously with our lives and living” — the statement is correct. The socio-economic life of the people of Bangladesh is highly dependent on nature and natural resources due to the climatic reasons described by stem. Therefore, as a result of climate change, there are many changes in people’s livelihoods. Climate-related frequent natural disasters, chronic floods, river erosion, etc. change the livelihood of people. There is a great impact of climate change on the lives and livelihoods of the people of Bangladesh. During the rainy season, due to the heavy rainfall under the influence of the southwest monsoon, the country produces more crops and fruits. In winter, robi crops like rice, wheat, tobacco, pulses, oilseeds, round potatoes, onions, garlic, coriander, etc., and various vegetables can be produced. However, severe winters often disrupt people’s normal lifestyles. Poor people suffer from a lack of work and money, and the southwest monsoon blows over the country during the summer. At this time, a large number of summer fruits such as mango, jam, litchi, jackfruit, and various juicy fruits are produced in Bangladesh. However, during the summer, monsoon storms often occur in this country. In addition, due to the low pressure created in the Bay of Bengal, the coastal region of this country often falls under the influence of various catastrophic cyclones. It causes extensive loss of life and property in coastal areas. As a result, many become destitute and move to urban areas in search of work. In the context of the overall discussion, it can be said that the climate is closely related to the livelihood of the people of Bangladesh.\n---","image":null,"image_url":null}]

The map illustrates Bangladesh’s topographical conditions. Except for the hilly areas in the northeastern and southeastern parts, nearly the entire country consists of riverine plains. Based on topography, Bangladesh can be primarily divided into three categories: Tertiary-period Mountains, Pleistocene terraces, and recent floodplains. Approximately 12% of Bangladesh’s total land area is covered by Tertiary period mountains. These mountains were created about 2 million years ago during the rise of the Himalayas. The hills of this region are divided into two parts: the southeastern mountains and the northern and northeastern mountains. About 8% of Bangladesh’s total land area is made up of Pleistocene terraces. The Pleistocene period, which occurred around 25,000 years ago, is thought to have formed these terraces due to flooding from melting glaciers. The Pleistocene terraces are further divided into three areas: Barind, Madhupur, and Bhawal’s ridges, and Lalmai hills. Around 80% of Bangladesh’s land consists of a vast floodplain created by rivers. Due to numerous rivers flowing across the flat land, floods occur during the rainy season. Year after year, silt carried by the floodwaters accumulates, forming the recent floodplain. The soil layer here is deep and the land is very fertile. This fertile land supports good crop production, contributing to the country’s overall economic development. According to experts, Bangladesh is located in one of the world’s major earthquake zones. Earthquakes occur in Bangladesh due to the collision of tectonic plates. Bangladesh lies between the tectonically active Indian Plate and the Myanmar Sub-Plate. According to geologists, there are significant faults or fractures in the northern and eastern parts of Bangladesh where earthquakes can occur. These faults are connected to the \"Deadly Danger Fault\". The Sylhet district of Bangladesh is located on this dangerous fault line. In 1989, a French engineering consortium created a map of Bangladesh’s earthquake zone. It showed three types of zones: terribly disturbing, dangerous, and venial. These zones are called 'Seismic Risk Zones'. In the terribly disturbing seismic risk zone, the districts of Bandarban, Chittagong, Sylhet, Mymensingh, and Rangpur are located. The dangerous seismic risk zones include Dhaka, Tangali, Bogura, Dinajpur, Cumilla, and Ranganati. Bangladesh is geographically located in a place where geologists predict that earthquakes of magnitude eight or higher could occur at any time. If an earthquake occurs in Bangladesh, the level of damage will be high due to unplanned buildings, negligence in constructing earthquake-resistant buildings, and lack of awareness and preparedness regarding earthquakes. The fault line under Bangladesh, from Sylhet to the hilly region of Cox's Bazar, is particularly vulnerable to earthquakes of magnitude eight or higher, which could cause devastating damage. According to a study, if even one percent of the buildings in the Dhaka Metropolitan area are destroyed by an earthquake, 6,000 buildings will collapse, and at least 300,000 people will be directly affected. Moreover, in unplanned cities, rescue and service operations after an earthquake would be hindered, creating even more risks for people’s lives. Additionally, densely populated areas like Narayanganj, Savar, and Gazipur would be further affected, with hundreds of thousands of people suffering. Without prior preparation, it will be extremely difficult to carry out emergency rescue operations in these densely populated areas after an earthquake. If no plans are in place, it will be impossible to manage essential tasks like emergency medical care, electricity, and water supply, leading to a humanitarian disaster.
